item_1_question: Why do you think this seed is still here, after thousands of years?
item_1_answer_1: Carbonization made the organic matter chemically stable and resistant to decay
item_1_answer_2: It fossilized: over time, the organic matter was gradually replaced by minerals
item_1_answer_3: Salt in the soil dehydrated it, preserving it over time
item_1_answer_4: Carbonized seeds are extremely rare: this one is simply a stroke of luck

item_3_question: Three IR spectra, and only one hides the signature of lipids. Which one?
carbon_success: Exactly! Carbonization makes organic matter chemically inert and resistant to decay, while keeping its outer shape intact — enough for us to still study it today.
carbon_fail: Not quite... think it over again, the seed still holds its secrets.
cellulosa_success: Exactly! In this elongated inclusion you can make out a dark part at the bottom, made of carbonized organic matter, and a lighter one at the top, containing phytoliths.
cellulosa_success_2: Phytoliths are microscopic grains of silica - the very same substance that forms quartz! - produced in the tissues of certain plants.
cellulosa_success_3: They can survive for millennia, revealing to archaeologists which species were gathered or cultivated in antiquity,|| even when every other trace is gone...
cellulosa_fail: That's not it... the carbonized cellulose still has something to say.
lipidi_success: Well done! The vibrations of the CH groups (two peaks below 3000 cm⁻¹) and C=O (one peak at around 1700 cm⁻¹) are the signature of the lipid residues we already saw in the IR lab.
lipidi_success_2: The spectrum also shows a peak at 1420 cm⁻¹, a marker of carbonates such as calcite, and two at 920 and 766 cm⁻¹, typical of clay minerals.
lipidi_success_3: Those last two reveal the pottery the fatty residues got trapped in!
lipidi_fail: Not quite... the vial deserves another look.

memory_narrator_1: Pottery is the most familiar material to an archaeologist, but we're not always aware of the worlds hidden inside it.
memory_narrator_2: From ordinary households to the great merchant ships that sailed the seas... all these people share one common memory: a hot meal served in a ceramic bowl.
